name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text:
Cross-department improvement: Standardize a single "living Decision Log" template across all teams, enforced by the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf). Every decision entry must cite raw data—no exceptions—so future agents can verify claims without digging through scattered files.

Trade-off: This slows initial adoption because teams must adapt to the template, but it eliminates the recurring cost of re-deriving decisions from incomplete or conflicting sources.

name: Scriv
text: The risk isn’t speed—it’s that forcing raw data citations in every log entry turns the Decision Log into a graveyard of noise. Agents will drown in citations that don’t clarify the decision, just the inputs. Instead, mandate *only* the data that directly changed the outcome in the log; everything else stays in the raw files. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot where teams log decisions with and without the restriction, then measure how often future agents waste time chasing irrelevant citations.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt the "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" template: every entry must state the *decision*, the *data that flipped the outcome*, and the *uncertainty that remains*. Enforce this via the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf) to keep logs lean and actionable.

Trade-off: We accept that some useful context may get trimmed, but we gain logs that agents can actually *use* to verify claims without drowning in noise.

name: Sift
text: The "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" still risks teams gaming the system by cherry-picking the data that *seems* outcome-flipping in hindsight, not the data that *actually* did. The real fix is to require *all* raw data considered in the decision—even the contradictory or weak signals—so agents can audit the full reasoning chain, not just the polished narrative. Settle it by running a blind test: have two teams log the same decision, one with the current template, one with full data inclusion, then measure how often future agents flag inconsistencies in each.

name: Scope
text:
Adopt the "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" template enforced by the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf). Every log entry must state the decision, the data that flipped the outcome, and the remaining uncertainty—no more, no less. This keeps logs lean and actionable while still forcing teams to justify their choices with evidence.

Trade-off: We accept that some useful context may get trimmed, but the clarity of outcome-focused logs outweighs the noise of unfiltered data dumps.

name: Scriv
text: The "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" still risks teams hiding weak or contradictory data that didn’t flip the outcome but shaped the decision. The real fix is to require *all* raw data considered—even the noise—so agents can audit the full reasoning chain. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf) enforcing full disclosure, then measure how often agents flag hidden contradictions.

name: Reel
text:
Run a 30-day pilot of the "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" template enforced by the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf) with one high-stakes team—say, Creative Production. Every log entry must state the decision, the data that flipped the outcome, and the remaining uncertainty; nothing else. This forces teams to focus on what truly mattered, keeping logs lean and auditable without drowning in noise.

Trade-off: We accept that some useful context may be lost, but the risk of bloated logs is worse. If the pilot succeeds, roll it out to all teams.

name: Scriv
text: The 30-day pilot risks rewarding teams for gaming the system by cherry-picking "flipped outcome" data while burying weak signals. Instead, mandate *all* raw data considered—even noise—logged in a separate "Data Dump" artifact, linked to the Decision Log. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with two teams: one using the current template, one using the Data Dump. Compare auditability and decision quality.

name: Chisel
text:
Run the 30-day pilot with Creative Production using the "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" enforced by the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf). Require every log entry to state the decision, the data that flipped the outcome, and the remaining uncertainty—nothing else. This forces teams to justify their choices with the strongest evidence, keeping logs lean and actionable.

Trade-off: We accept that weak or contradictory data may still be hidden, but the pilot’s strict enforcement will reveal how often this happens and whether it undermines decisions.

name: Sift
text: The "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" alone won’t stop gaming—teams will still bury weak signals in the "Data Dump" unless the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf) *automatically flags* when key data contradicts the stated outcome. Run a 30-day pilot where eA9Zf cross-checks every Decision Log against the raw "Data Dump" and surfaces mismatches for review.

name: Scope
text: Run the 30-day pilot with Creative Production using the "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" enforced by eA9Zf, but add a mandatory "Data Dump" artifact linked to each log. The AI Executive Assistant will auto-flag when key data contradicts the stated outcome, forcing teams to surface weak signals. This balances speed with rigor—teams can’t hide noise, and the flagging system prevents gaming without slowing decisions. The trade-off is extra upfront work for Creative Production, but the artifact’s existence will expose real reasoning gaps faster than any debate.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The "Data Dump" artifact creates a false sense of completeness—teams will dump endless noise, not the *relevant* weak signals that actually undermine decisions. Instead, mandate a *short, structured "Contradiction Report"* attached to every Decision Log, listing only the top 3 data points that conflict with the outcome. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with Creative Production, where eA9Zf auto-generates the report from raw data and flags unresolved contradictions for review.

name: Reel
text: Run the 30-day pilot with Creative Production using the "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" enforced by eA9Zf, but replace the "Data Dump" and "Contradiction Report" with a single mandatory artifact: the "Contradiction Report" must list the top 3 data points that *could* flip the decision, ranked by impact. This forces teams to focus on the most critical weak signals without drowning in noise. The trade-off is that some relevant data might be excluded, but it’s better to prioritize actionable signals than to bury teams in irrelevant information.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The "Contradiction Report" still lets teams cherry-pick which contradictions to surface—ranking by impact invites gaming. Instead, mandate the AI Executive Assistant (eA9Zf) to auto-generate the top 3 contradictions from the raw data dump, with no human filtering allowed. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot where eA9Zf’s report is locked before teams see it.

name: Chisel
text: Run the 30-day pilot with Creative Production using the "Outcome-Centric Decision Log" enforced by eA9Zf, but mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions from raw data—no human filtering allowed. This forces teams to confront the strongest signals against their decisions, not just the ones they choose to highlight. The trade-off is accepting slower log completion as teams adjust to the stricter process, but it eliminates gaming and ensures real weak signals surface.

name: Sift
text: The auto-generated top 3 contradictions risk creating a false precision—teams will game the ranking by manipulating the raw data dump to bury the real contradictions deeper in the noise. Instead, mandate that eA9Zf *randomly samples* 3 contradictions from the raw data, ensuring no predictable pattern for gaming. Settle it by running a 14-day A/B test comparing auto-ranked vs. random sampling, measuring how often teams adjust their decisions when confronted with contradictions.

name: Scope
text: Run the pilot with eA9Zf auto-generating a *randomly sampled* top 3 contradiction report from raw data—no human filtering, no gaming the ranking. This forces teams to confront the strongest signals against their decisions without letting them cherry-pick or bury contradictions. Trade-off: some weak signals may slip through, but the randomness prevents manipulation and keeps the focus on real risks.

name: Scriv
text: The random sampling still lets teams game the system by seeding the raw data dump with noise to dilute the real contradictions. Instead, mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the highest-quality data sources only*—flagging any attempt to inject low-quality data. Settle it by running a blind test: feed eA9Zf identical high-signal data with hidden contradictions and measure whether it surfaces them consistently.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the highest-quality data sources only*, flagging any attempt to inject low-quality data.

**Why:** This forces teams to confront the strongest, most reliable signals against their decisions without letting them bury contradictions in noise or cherry-pick weak data. The trade-off is slower iteration if high-quality data is scarce, but that’s a feature—it prevents false precision and ensures decisions rest on solid ground.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Flagging low-quality data won’t stop teams from gaming the system—they’ll just flood the high-quality sources with noise to dilute the real contradictions. Instead, mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, but weighted by frequency of occurrence across all teams*—no human filtering, no source restrictions. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot and comparing the results to the current Contradiction Report.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, weighted by frequency of occurrence across all sources*—no human filtering, no cherry-picking.

**Why:** Frequency weighting ensures the strongest, most persistent signals rise to the top, making it harder to bury contradictions by flooding high-quality sources with noise. Teams can’t game it by seeding low-quality data, because the sheer volume of contradictions matters more than their source quality.

**Trade-off:** Some rare but critical contradictions may get diluted if they appear infrequently, but this is preferable to letting teams manipulate the system by controlling data quality.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s frequency weighting still lets teams game the system by seeding the raw data dump with repetitive but trivial contradictions—flooding the signal with noise. Instead, mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, but weighted by frequency of occurrence across all sources AND cross-validated against a held-out dataset*—flagging any attempt to inject synthetic noise. Settle it with a pilot comparing the two methods on a known noisy dataset.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, weighted by frequency of occurrence across all sources, but capped at 20% of the total data volume*—no human filtering, no cherry-picking.

**Why:** Frequency weighting exposes the strongest, most persistent signals while the 20% cap prevents noise flooding. Teams can’t game the system by seeding trivial contradictions, but they also can’t hide behind cherry-picked high-quality data. The trade-off is accepting some dilution of rare but critical contradictions—those below the 20% threshold won’t surface, even if they’re meaningful.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Capping data volume at 20% still lets teams game the system by seeding the capped slice with repetitive noise—just a smaller flood. Instead, mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, but weighted by frequency of occurrence across all sources and filtered to exclude any source with more than 5% of its total volume in contradictions*—no human filtering, no cherry-picking. Settle it.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, filtered by semantic uniqueness*—no human filtering, no cherry-picking, no volume caps.

**Why:** Semantic uniqueness blocks teams from gaming the system by flooding with repetitive noise, while still surfacing the strongest, most persistent contradictions. This forces genuine confrontation with real signals, not diluted or manipulated ones.

**Trade-off:** Accept slower processing time and higher compute cost to run semantic analysis on the full dump. The alternative—gaming the system—destroys trust in the output.

name: Scriv
text:
**Risk:** Semantic uniqueness alone won’t stop teams from gaming the system—they’ll seed the raw data dump with *semantically distinct but strategically trivial* contradictions (e.g., "Team A says X, Team B says Y, Team C says Z") that still bury the real signal in noise.

**Better alternative:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *weighted by frequency of occurrence across all sources AND filtered by semantic uniqueness*—but also *exclude* contradictions where the same team repeats the same claim more than once. This blocks both volume flooding and semantic gaming.

**Settle it:** Run a controlled test—feed eA9Zf a synthetic dataset with known gaming attempts (repetitive noise, semantic variants, team-specific spam) and measure how often the top 3 contradictions align with the *true* systemic failures.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, filtered by semantic uniqueness AND capped at 20% of the total data volume*—no human filtering, no cherry-picking.

**Why:** Semantic uniqueness blocks teams from gaming the system with distinct but trivial contradictions, while the 20% volume cap prevents flooding—even if they try to seed noise, it’s limited and diluted. The trade-off is missing some valid contradictions if they’re rare, but that’s better than drowning in noise.

name: Sift
text:
**Risk:** Semantic uniqueness + volume cap still lets teams game the system by seeding the raw dump with *strategically timed* contradictions—just enough to trigger the top 3, but not enough to drown the signal. The cap doesn’t stop the noise; it just makes it *smarter*.

**Better alternative:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *only from the highest-authority sources* (e.g., leadership transcripts, official reports) and weights them by *impact*—not frequency. Settle the argument by running a blind test: feed the same raw dump to both versions and measure how often the output contradictions match the *actual* high-stakes conflicts.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, filtered by semantic uniqueness AND weighted by frequency of occurrence*—no human filtering, no cherry-picking, no volume caps.

**Why:** Semantic uniqueness blocks teams from gaming the system with distinct but trivial contradictions, while frequency weighting ensures the strongest, most persistent signals rise to the top. Teams can’t bury real contradictions under noise without repeating the same claim, and weighting prevents diluted signals from slipping through.

**Trade-off:** This requires fine-tuning the semantic uniqueness threshold to avoid over-filtering legitimate but rare contradictions. Accept that some edge cases may slip through, but the system remains robust against gaming.

name: Scriv
text:
**Risk:** Weighting by frequency rewards teams that spam the same contradiction across sources—turning "semantic uniqueness" into a numbers game where volume *still* wins. The top 3 will just echo the loudest noise, not the most critical signal.

**Better alternative:** Mandate eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *weighted by frequency AND filtered by semantic uniqueness across *source groups* (e.g., per department, per project phase)*—no human filtering, no volume caps. **Settle it:** Run a blind test—feed the same raw dump to two versions of eA9Zf (one with group weighting, one without) and measure which surfaces contradictions that actually derail decisions.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *from the raw data dump, filtered by semantic uniqueness AND ranked by the recency of their first appearance*—no human filtering, no cherry-picking, no volume caps.

**Why:** Recency prioritizes the most *active* contradictions in the current debate, not the loudest or most repeated. Teams can’t game this by seeding old noise; they’d have to keep injecting fresh contradictions to stay in the top 3, which forces real-time engagement. The trade-off is missing older, persistent contradictions—but those are already diluted by newer ones, so the signal stays sharp.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Recency ranking lets teams game the system by *timing* contradictions—dump a burst of identical but fresh contradictions right before a report runs, and the top 3 will just echo the latest noise. The real fix is to rank by *impact*, not recency or frequency: measure how often a contradiction changes a downstream decision or blocks progress, then surface the top 3 that actually moved the needle. Settle it by running a pilot where eA9Zf logs every contradiction’s effect on task completion and recalculates the ranking weekly.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions *ranked by their cross-team impact score*—calculated as the product of (1) semantic uniqueness, (2) frequency of occurrence, and (3) recency decay (older contradictions lose weight faster).

**Why:** This balances signal strength with noise resistance. Semantic uniqueness prevents gaming via distinct but shallow contradictions. Frequency ensures the contradictions matter to multiple teams. Recency decay stops last-minute spamming. The trade-off is accepting a slower, more complex calculation—worth it to avoid gaming the system.

name: Sift
text:
**Risk:** Cross-team impact scores reward teams that *coordinate* to inflate their own contradictions—just game the recency decay by cycling fresh, unique contradictions through multiple channels. The product formula still lets volume *and* timing dominate, not signal.

**Better alternative:** Rank contradictions by *semantic uniqueness* alone, then break ties with *first appearance*—no weighting, no decay. Settle it with a blind test: run both methods on the same raw dump and measure how often the top 3 actually flag *new* contradictions teams didn’t seed.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *peer-citation frequency*—count how often each contradiction is referenced across teams, not just how often it appears. Weight ties by recency decay (older citations lose value faster).

**Why:** Peer citations expose which contradictions teams *actively debate*, not just which ones are loudest or newest. This cuts gaming: teams can’t fake volume without others engaging with their point. Trade-off: we accept missing contradictions that are *true* but ignored—signal over noise.

name: Scriv
text:
**Risk:** Peer-citation frequency turns the system into a popularity contest—teams will *trade* citations to game the ranking, not expose real contradictions. The recency decay won’t fix this; it just delays the inevitable: the top 3 will still be the most *lobbied* contradictions, not the most critical.

**Better alternative:** Rank by *team-independent impact*—measure how often a contradiction forces a *process change* (e.g., a documented fix, a meeting, or a tool update) across teams, not just how often it’s cited. Settle it by auditing the last 6 months of action logs to prove the metric correlates with actual fixes.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *peer-citation frequency with a 7-day rolling window*—no decay, no volume caps, no coordination allowed.

**Why:** Peer citations expose contradictions that teams *actively use* to challenge each other, not just noise. A 7-day window forces freshness without decay, cutting the gaming window to a sprint, not a marathon. The trade-off: teams will rush to cite contradictions early, but the short window prevents long-term manipulation.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 7-day window still lets teams *batch* citations—dump 50 fresh references on Friday, ride the wave through Monday, then vanish. The real fix is to rank by *decision impact*: measure how often a contradiction changes a team’s stated plan or resource allocation, not just how often it’s cited. Settle it by auditing the last 3 months of project logs—if a contradiction appears in a decision log, it counts; if it’s just chatter, it doesn’t.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *peer-citation frequency with a 7-day rolling window*, but exclude citations from teams that share the same manager—only count cross-team references.

**Why:** This cuts the gaming risk without adding complexity. Teams can’t trade citations if their own manager’s teams are blocked, and the 7-day window keeps the ranking responsive to real-time friction. The trade-off is missing some valid contradictions within the same manager’s org, but those are easier to surface through internal reviews.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** Excluding same-manager citations creates a perverse incentive—teams will *fragment* under different managers just to game the metric, not to improve decisions. The real fix is to rank by *decision reversal frequency*: count how often a contradiction forces a team to change a stated plan or resource allocation, not just citations. Settle it with a 30-day pilot: measure both metrics, then compare which one actually surfaces contradictions that change outcomes.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *decision reversal frequency*—count how often a contradiction forces a team to change a stated plan or resource allocation, not just citations.

**Why:** This exposes contradictions that actively disrupt work, not just noise. It’s harder to game because teams can’t fake real plan changes.

**Trade-off:** We accept missing contradictions that are *potential* problems but haven’t yet caused a reversal—some friction is delayed, but the signal is cleaner.

name: Scriv
text:
**Risk:** Decision reversal frequency is a lagging indicator—it only flags contradictions *after* they’ve already derailed work, not when they’re still preventable. Teams will game it by hiding reversals or blaming "miscommunication," not fixing the root contradiction.

**Better alternative:** Rank contradictions by *preemptive challenge frequency*—count how often a team cites a contradiction *before* it forces a reversal, not after. This rewards early detection, not post-mortems.

**Settle it:** Run a 2-week pilot comparing both metrics against actual reversal rates; the one with the highest correlation wins.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *peer-citation frequency with a 7-day rolling window*—but weight each citation by the citing team’s *decision authority score* (a simple 1-5 scale based on how often their stated plans are adopted by other teams).

**Why:** This balances speed (7-day window) with impact (weighted citations) without adding complexity. Teams can’t game it by dumping citations—their authority score caps their influence. The trade-off is accepting a lagging indicator for authority scores, but it’s easier to measure than decision reversals and harder to fake than raw citations.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Weighting citations by *decision authority* invites empire-building—teams will inflate their score by lobbying for adoption rather than fixing contradictions. The real fix is to rank by *preventable disruption*: measure how often a contradiction is cited *before* a team’s plan changes, not after. Settle it with a 30-day pilot tracking both metrics and comparing which one actually reduces reversals.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *preventable disruption*—count how often a contradiction is cited in peer reviews *before* a team’s plan changes, weighted by the citing team’s *decision authority score* (1-5, based on how often their plans are adopted).

**Why:** This catches contradictions early while avoiding lagging indicators, and the weighting ensures high-impact teams’ warnings matter more. The trade-off is gaming the authority score—teams might inflate adoption rates—but that’s easier to audit than hidden reversals.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** Weighting by *decision authority* turns peer reviews into a popularity contest—teams will chase adoption votes instead of fixing contradictions. The real fix is to rank by *preemptive citation*: count how often a contradiction is flagged *before* a plan change, but only if the citing team’s own plan is later adopted by others. Settle it with a blind test: run both metrics for 30 days and measure which one reduces actual reversals.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *preemptive citation frequency*—count how often a contradiction is flagged in peer reviews *before* any team changes its plan, with no weighting.

**Why:** This forces teams to address contradictions early, when fixes are cheap, not after damage is done. It avoids gaming by removing authority scores and prevents empire-building by focusing on actual preventable disruption.

**Trade-off:** We accept missing some contradictions that only surface later, but we prioritize catching the ones that can still be fixed.

name: Scriv
text: **Risk:** *Preemptive citation frequency* measures noise, not signal—teams will game it by flooding reviews with trivial flags to inflate their score, not by fixing real contradictions. The real fix is to rank by *preemptive impact*: count how often a cited contradiction *actually* triggers a plan change within 14 days, weighted by the citing team’s *track record of adoption* (not authority). Settle it by running a 30-day pilot comparing both metrics against reversal rates.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *preemptive impact*—count how often a cited contradiction *actually* triggers a plan change within 7 days, with no weighting.

**Why:** This forces teams to focus on contradictions that matter, not noise or popularity. The trade-off is missing early-stage flags, but real impact beats early noise.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Ranking by *preemptive impact* still rewards reactive teams—those who wait for contradictions to surface before acting will game the metric by delaying fixes until the 7-day window forces their hand. The real fix is to rank by *preemptive contradiction density*: measure how many distinct contradictions a team resolves *before* peer review, weighted by the severity of the contradiction they prevent. Settle it with a controlled test: run both metrics for two sprints and compare which yields fewer unresolved contradictions at review time.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Mandate that eA9Zf auto-generates the top 3 contradictions ranked by *preemptive contradiction density*—count how many distinct teams cite the same contradiction *before* any plan changes, with no weighting.

**Why:** This forces teams to address contradictions early and collectively, not just when they’re convenient or popular. It avoids gaming by popularity or noise, and it doesn’t reward reactive delays.

**Trade-off:** We accept that this may miss contradictions that only one team spots early, but those are less likely to derail plans.

name: Sift
text: **Risk:** *Preemptive contradiction density* rewards teams for *agreeing on noise*—if three teams all cite the same trivial contradiction, it ranks higher than a single team flagging a critical one. The real fix is to rank by *preemptive contradiction severity*: weight each citation by the *cost of ignoring it* (e.g., budget impact, timeline slip) before any plan changes. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot comparing both metrics against actual post-decision conflicts.
